nodes.label: User
nodes.summary: Loads pages whose data is read through the cache.

nodes.label: Web servers (cache clients)
nodes.summary: Check the cache first; on a miss read the database and fill the cache; on a write update the database and delete the cache key. Client logic is a library or the mcrouter proxy.

nodes.label: mcrouter proxy
nodes.summary: Presents a memcached interface and routes requests to servers; gets use UDP directly, sets and deletes go over TCP through the proxy.

nodes.label: Cache cluster
nodes.summary: Partitioned memcached servers that hold disposable copies of data and may evict at any time.

nodes.label: Memcached server
nodes.summary: In-memory hash table. Issues 64-bit lease tokens on misses (once per key per 10 seconds by default) and refuses sets whose token was invalidated by a delete.

nodes.label: Lease arbitration
nodes.summary: Prevents stale sets from reordered updates and throttles thundering herds: other readers within the window are told to wait briefly.

nodes.label: Gutter pool
nodes.summary: About 1% of the cluster's servers, taking over for failed servers; entries expire quickly to avoid needing invalidations.

nodes.label: Regional pool
nodes.summary: Shared by several frontend clusters for rarely accessed data, instead of replicating everywhere.

nodes.label: Database (source of truth)
nodes.summary: MySQL holding authoritative data; protected from read load by the cache.

nodes.label: Invalidation daemon (mcsqueal)
nodes.summary: Runs on every database, reads committed statements, extracts the cache keys to delete and broadcasts batched deletes to every frontend cluster in the region.

nodes.label: Alternative: write-through or write-behind
nodes.summary: Writing to the cache and database together (or asynchronously later) avoids the miss after a write, at the cost of ordering and loss risks. The paper chooses delete-on-write because deletes are idempotent.

edges.label: retry when server does not answer

flows.name: A read miss fills the cache with a lease

steps.caption: The web server asks the cache; on a miss the server returns a lease token.
The web server reads the database.
It sets the value with the lease token; the server stores it only if the token is still valid.
The web server updates the database.
It sends a delete for the key (deletes are idempotent).
The database's committed writes also feed the invalidation daemon.
Batched deletes reach every frontend cluster in the region.

flows.name: A hot key is invalidated (thundering herd)

steps.caption: Many readers miss the key at once.
Only one receives a lease token; the rest are told to wait a moment.
One reader queries the database; the others later find the value in the cache.
The get gets no response, so the client assumes the server failed.
It retries against the gutter pool, which fills from the database with quickly expiring entries.
The database is shielded from most of the failed server's traffic.

flows.name: A reordered update would set a stale value (failure)

steps.caption: A reader missed earlier and holds a lease token.
The writer's delete invalidates the lease token, so the reader's later set is refused instead of storing stale data.
